questions.question: In a Sparse Merkle Tree used as a key→value map, what determines a key’s leaf position?
options: The insertion order of keys into the tree
A deterministic function of the key (typically a hash) and the fixed tree depth
The hash of the value stored at that key
The current root hash of the tree
questions.explanation: SMTs map each key to a fixed leaf index derived from the key (often via hashing), independent of insertion order.

questions.question: For a binary Merkle proof of one leaf, what information is typically needed to recompute the root?
options: Only the root hash and the leaf value
All other leaves in the dataset
A list of sibling hashes along the path from the leaf to the root
A digital signature over the leaf value
questions.explanation: A Merkle proof supplies the sibling hashes needed to hash upward and reconstruct the committed root.

questions.question: Why do we domain-separate leaf hashing from internal-node hashing in Merkle-style trees?
options: To make SHA-256 run faster on short inputs
To prevent treating an internal node hash as a valid leaf encoding (a second-preimage style confusion)
To ensure the tree can only store UTF-8 values
To reduce the number of hashes needed in a proof
questions.explanation: Without domain separation, an attacker may be able to present an internal-node hash as if it were a leaf, confusing verification.

questions.question: In this lesson’s SMT, how is the empty tree root computed for depth d?
options: It is always 32 bytes of zeros, regardless of hashing rules
It is the hash of the string "empty"
It is computed by repeatedly hashing the default leaf hash with itself up to level d
It is undefined until at least one key is inserted
questions.explanation: We precompute default/empty hashes bottom-up: default[0]=empty leaf, default[i+1]=H(default[i],default[i]).

questions.question: How does an SMT non-inclusion proof work in this lesson’s model?
options: The prover signs a statement that the key is missing
The prover shows a Merkle path where the leaf value is the default empty value
The prover reveals all keys currently present in the tree
Non-inclusion proofs are impossible with Merkle trees
questions.explanation: Non-inclusion is proven by showing the leaf at the key’s deterministic index is the canonical empty value, with a normal proof path.

questions.question: In the toy RSA-accumulator-style vector commitment, which check verifies an opening at index i?
options: H(value) == commitment
witness^p_i mod n == commitment, where p_i is the prime derived from (i,value)
witness + p_i == commitment
commitment^p_i mod n == witness
questions.explanation: The witness is g^(product of all primes except p_i); raising it to p_i reconstructs the full commitment.

questions.question: What replaces the 'sibling hash list' in a Verkle-style proof path?
options: A signature from a trusted third party for each level
A short opening (witness) that the chosen child value is at the correct index in the parent’s committed vector
A full copy of the parent node’s entire child vector
A random nonce that the verifier later reveals
questions.explanation: Verkle-style trees use vector commitments so the prover can open one child position without sending all siblings.

questions.question: What is the main depth/width tradeoff behind using a high branching factor (e.g., 256) in Verkle-style designs?
options: Higher width increases depth but makes hashing faster
Higher width reduces depth, so fewer levels must be proven, at the cost of more expensive per-node commitments/openings
Width does not affect proof size or computation
Higher width eliminates the need for hashing entirely
questions.explanation: A wider tree has fewer levels for the same key space, but each node handles a larger vector commitment and related operations.
